prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on the magic-wavelength principle, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Reading the opening ballots, B015 is the one candidate that nearly every colleague ranks highly (all eight rank it, five place it in their top three), and I now think I under-ranked it at sixth. Katori's magic-wavelength idea is a clean mechanism: choose the lattice wavelength so the light shift cancels for both clock states, and a many-body ensemble becomes a frequency reference. Ye's group then showed what the idea can do, including the 10^-18 regime, control of every systematic shift, and clocks that are themselves a many-body system with spin-exchange physics. The attribution is a clear two-person split between originator and perfecter. Several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL) reproduce and compare the clocks, so the interpretation is stable. This sits well with what I look for: a simple idea that is understood and then confirmed at extreme precision. The impact on tests of constants, relativistic geodesy and the pending redefinition of the second is concrete.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is that the physics prize record already contains neighbouring work: Hall and Hansch (2005) for the frequency comb and Wineland (2012) for control of single trapped ions, whose ion clocks are direct competitors. A reasonable colleague can argue that the optical lattice clock is a superb refinement of a recognised toolbox rather than a new phenomenon. It is also an instrument achievement more than a discovery of a new principle of nature. The redefinition of the second has not happened yet, which cuts both ways. Finally, I put fluctuation theorems (B005) first on my own ballot because they are a deeper, more universal statement, and nobody else ranked them; that tells me my enthusiasm may reflect my own field's taste more than the committee's weighing of maturity and credit, and the attribution there (Gallavotti, Cohen, Kurchan, Lebowitz-Spohn, Hatano-Sasa are not on the list) is honestly unsettled.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth ranks B015 first: precision atomic physics at its best, a clear idea and decisive experiment with a thorough understanding of every systematic, and a clean two-laureate configuration, with the comb prize of 2005 as backdrop rather than overlap.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution and on the quality of the systematics, and this has moved me up from sixth. Where I would qualify your point is on novelty: the committee should be explicit that the citation is for the lattice-clock principle and the many-body regime, not for clocks in general, otherwise the 2005 and 2012 prizes make the claim look thin. If the citation names the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 regime I find your case convincing, and I see no need to wait for the formal redefinition of the second.

responses.point: Eva Olsson ranks the topological-insulator entry B003 (Kane, Molenkamp, Xue) first, arguing that Kane's theory, Molenkamp's HgTe observation and Xue's quantum anomalous Hall measurement make a theory plus two decisive experiments, mature and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I accept the scientific weight but I disagree with the three-way split. Xue's quantum anomalous Hall result is a separate achievement and the credited trio drops Mele, whose joint work with Kane produced the Z2 classification and the graphene prediction, and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang's HgTe proposal preceded Molenkamp's experiment. Pearce's two-name version is cleaner but loses Mele; my own B018 triple (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) is the most defensible theory-plus-experiment unit, but with Zhang deceased and Hasan outside it the credit problem is real. I keep topological insulators as a strong alternative, not my first choice, because the allocation is more contested than for B015, and the 2016 topological-phase prize overlaps.

responses.point: Ulf Danielsson ranks IceCube (B014) first: a discovery given to us by nature, the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux and the TXS 0506+056 association, opening a new window and bearing on cosmic-ray origin.
responses.response: I share your preference for nature giving a clue, and the flux is established well above five sigma. My doubt is attribution rather than science: a large collaboration, with AMANDA, Baikal and ANTARES history, being reduced to two names, which you also flag yourself. I also read the source identification as still partial (two individually significant sources). I could support B014 if the committee is comfortable with the Halzen-Karle pairing, but I cannot judge IceCube internals as a theorist of complex systems, so I will not push either way.

responses.point: Olle Eriksson ranks B003 first and puts magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B030) third, valuing the pairing of a theoretical prediction (flat bands) with a clear experimental discovery.
responses.response: I like the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model for the same reason you do: a simple model explaining a messy system. But you note yourself that the mechanism of the superconductivity is unsettled and the field is only about eight years old, and the allocation question (Dean, Kim, Yacoby, Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) is open. I would not move B030 into the preferred configuration yet; waiting a few more years costs little.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the optical lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether the pending SI second redefinition should affect timing.

Whether fluctuation theorems (B005) can be given a defensible three-person attribution given the Gallavotti-Cohen, Kurchan, Lebowitz-Spohn and Hatano-Sasa competing claims; if only one person (Jarzynski) were credited it would not fit the supplied list entry.
How to resolve the topological-insulator credit (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Xue, Hasan, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang) in B003 versus B018, given the 2016 prize overlap.
How much weight a co-opted member should carry in the final vote is not clear from my role.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: none of the credited candidates for B015 is a known collaborator or institutional colleague. My closest ties are to turbulent aerosols and random-matrix theory, and the fluctuation-theorem entry I ranked first (B005) has no listed connection to my frequent co-authors; the Gothenburg link to Chalmers colleagues is institutional only.
